# Missing data {#sec-missing}

```{r}
#| label: setup-ch11
#| include: false
library(survival)
library(mice)
library(MatchIt)
library(MatchThem)
library(cobalt)
library(dplyr)
source("R/simulate_cohort.R")
cohort <- simulate_cohort(n = 2000, seed = 2026)
```

{{< include ./_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## You need this chapter if…
- `coxph()` reports that **observations were deleted due to missingness**, and it's more than a handful;
- a **confounder** you need for matching or adjustment has missing values;
- you're wondering whether to just analyse the complete cases.

*This chapter builds on Chapter 3, and on Chapters 5–7 for the section on matching.*
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## In this chapter
**The question.** Real datasets have gaps. What does R do with them by default, when does that give the wrong answer, and what should you do instead?

**By the end of this chapter you will be able to:**

- spot how many patients a model has silently dropped;
- explain the three kinds of missing data (MCAR, MAR, MNAR), and when a complete-case analysis is biased;
- carry out **multiple imputation** with the **mice** package, including the survival outcome correctly, and pool the results;
- combine multiple imputation with propensity score matching using **MatchThem**.
:::

## What R does by default

Most R modelling functions, including `coxph()`, quietly drop every row
with a missing value in *any* variable in the model. This is called a
**complete-case analysis**. In the `lung` data, a few variables have gaps:

```{r}
#| label: lung-missing
colSums(is.na(survival::lung))
```

Each gap looks small. But put several of these variables in one model:

```{r}
#| label: lung-cc
coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age + ph.ecog + wt.loss + meal.cal,
      data = survival::lung)
```

The last line of the output says it: 58 of the 228 patients (25%) were
dropped, and 42 of the 165 deaths. That costs precision, and, as the rest
of this chapter shows, it can also bias the results. Always check `n` and
`number of events` against the size of your data.

### Practice: how much has the model dropped?

*This is a live exercise: edit the code, click **Run Code**, and your answer is checked automatically. See @sec-live-exercises if you haven't used one before.*

Add `meal.cal` (calories eaten at meals) to a Cox model for the `lung`
data, and find out how many patients the model actually uses. Replace each
`______`, then click **Run Code**.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_cc_n
library(survival)
lung <- survival::lung
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_cc_n
#| caption: "Practice: how much has the model dropped?"
# Missing values in each column
colSums(is.na(lung))

# Cox model with meal.cal added
m <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age + ph.ecog + ______, data = lung)

# How many patients did the model use? (last line)
m$______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_cc_n"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1
The variable to add is `meal.cal`.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_cc_n"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2
The number of patients used is stored in `m$n`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_cc_n"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
colSums(is.na(lung))
m <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age + ph.ecog + meal.cal, data = lung)
m$n
```

`meal.cal` is missing for 47 patients, so the model uses only 180 of the
228 patients (and `ph.ecog` drops one more along the way). Nearly a fifth of
the data has gone, from a single variable with gaps.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_cc_n
#| check: true
m <- .envir_result$m
if (!inherits(m, "coxph") || !("meal.cal" %in% all.vars(formula(m)))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Add <code>meal.cal</code> to the model.")
} else if (!is.numeric(.result) || length(.result) != 1 || .result != m$n) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Make the last line <code>m$n</code>, the number of patients used.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("Correct! The model uses only %d of the 228 patients: %d were dropped because of missing values.", m$n, 228 - m$n))
}
```

## When does missing data cause bias?

It depends on **why** the values are missing. There are three kinds:

| Kind | Meaning | Example | Complete-case analysis |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MCAR**: missing completely at random | Whether a value is missing has nothing to do with the patient | A sample was lost in the post | Unbiased, but wastes data |
| **MAR**: missing at random | Whether a value is missing depends on things you **have** recorded | BMI is recorded less often for patients who died, and you know who died | Can be biased. Multiple imputation can fix it |
| **MNAR**: missing not at random | Whether a value is missing depends on the missing value itself, or on things you haven't recorded | Heavier patients avoid being weighed | Biased, and no standard method fully fixes it |

The names are confusing: "missing at random" doesn't mean the values are
missing randomly. It means they're missing at random **once you take
account of** the recorded information.

For a Cox model, one rule of thumb helps. If whether a covariate is
missing depends on the **outcome** (death, or how long patients survived),
a complete-case analysis is usually biased. If it depends only on other
covariates in the model, a complete-case analysis is usually fine, just less
precise.

## A demonstration with a known truth

We take the simulated cohort from Chapters 5–7 and delete some BMI values.
BMI is recorded less often for patients who **died** (perhaps their final
records were incomplete) and for **treated** patients (perhaps they were
managed at a different clinic):

```{r}
#| label: make-missing
set.seed(1)
p_miss <- plogis(-1.5 + 1.5 * cohort$status + 1 * cohort$treated)
cohort_miss <- cohort
cohort_miss$bmi[runif(nrow(cohort)) < p_miss] <- NA

mean(is.na(cohort_miss$bmi))                              # overall
tapply(is.na(cohort_miss$bmi), cohort_miss$status, mean)  # by death
tapply(is.na(cohort_miss$bmi), cohort_miss$treated, mean) # by treatment
```

38% of BMI values are now missing: 62% among patients who died, and 49%
among treated patients. This is **MAR**: the chance of being missing
depends on things we have recorded.

Compare the covariate-adjusted Cox model fitted to the full data, before
anything was deleted, with the complete-case analysis:

```{r}
#| label: cc-vs-full
covs <- "treated + age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker"
f <- as.formula(paste("Surv(time, status) ~", covs))

full_fit <- coxph(f, data = cohort)        # before deleting anything
cc_fit   <- coxph(f, data = cohort_miss)   # complete cases only

c(full = exp(coef(full_fit))[["treated"]],
  complete_case = exp(coef(cc_fit))[["treated"]])
cc_fit$n
```

With the full data, the treatment HR is 0.66 (the truth, which we built
into the data, is 0.70). The complete-case analysis uses only 1238 patients
and gives **0.50**, badly exaggerating the benefit. The patients it keeps
are not representative: treated patients who died are the most likely to
have been dropped.

## Multiple imputation

**Multiple imputation** fills in each missing value with a plausible value,
predicted from the patient's other information, plus some random variation
to reflect our uncertainty. It does this several times, making several
complete datasets that differ only in the filled-in values. Then:

1. **Impute:** create $m$ completed datasets (often 10 to 50).
2. **Analyse:** fit the same model to each one.
3. **Pool:** combine the $m$ results with **Rubin's rules**. The pooled
   estimate is the average of the $m$ estimates. Its standard error combines
   the uncertainty *within* each analysis with the variation *between* the
   imputed datasets, so the CI honestly reflects that some values were
   guessed.

The **mice** package does all three.

### Step 1: include the outcome, the right way

The imputation model must include **everything in the analysis model,
including the outcome**. It feels like cheating to use the outcome to fill
in a covariate, but leaving it out biases the results towards no effect.

For survival data, don't use the raw follow-up time. Instead, include the
event indicator (`status`) and the **Nelson–Aalen estimate** of the
cumulative hazard at each patient's follow-up time [@white2009]. `mice`
calculates it with `nelsonaalen()`:

```{r}
#| label: mi-prepare
cohort_miss$H <- nelsonaalen(cohort_miss, time, status)

# The variables used for imputation: the analysis variables, status and H
imp_data <- cohort_miss[, c("age", "female", "diabetes", "bmi", "smoker",
                            "treated", "status", "H", "time")]

# Keep time in the data (the Cox model needs it), but don't use it to impute
pred <- make.predictorMatrix(imp_data)
pred[, "time"] <- 0
```

### Step 2: impute

```{r}
#| label: mi-impute
imp <- mice(imp_data, m = 10, predictorMatrix = pred,
            seed = 1, printFlag = FALSE)
imp$method
```

`imp$method` shows how each variable is imputed. Only `bmi` has missing
values, and it uses `"pmm"` (*predictive mean matching*): each missing BMI
is replaced by an observed BMI from a patient with similar predicted
values, so the filled-in values are always realistic. `seed` makes the
result reproducible.

### Step 3: analyse and pool

```{r}
#| label: mi-pool
fit_mi <- with(imp, coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated + age + female +
                            diabetes + bmi + smoker))
pooled <- summary(pool(fit_mi), exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
pooled[, c("term", "estimate", "2.5 %", "97.5 %")]
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## How to read this output
- `with(imp, coxph(...))` fits the Cox model to each of the 10 completed datasets.
- `pool()` combines them with Rubin's rules, and `summary(..., exponentiate = TRUE)` reports hazard ratios.
- **estimate** is the pooled HR, and **2.5 %** and **97.5 %** its 95% CI.
:::

The pooled HR for treatment is **0.67** (95% CI 0.56 to 0.80), close to
the full-data value of 0.66, using all 2000 patients. Multiple imputation
has removed the bias that the complete-case analysis introduced.

### Practice: multiple imputation

*This is a live exercise: edit the code, click **Run Code**, and your answer is checked automatically. See @sec-live-exercises if you haven't used one before.*

The data with missing BMI values are prepared as in this chapter:
`imp_data` (including `status` and the Nelson–Aalen estimate `H`) and the
predictor matrix `pred`. Impute **5** datasets, fit the Cox model to each,
and pool the results. The first run downloads the mice package, which can
take a minute. Replace each `______`, then click **Run Code**.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_mi
if (!requireNamespace("mice", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("mice", quiet = TRUE)
library(survival)
library(mice)
simulate_cohort <- function(n = 2000, hr_treat = 0.70, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  age      <- round(pmin(pmax(rnorm(n, 65, 10), 35), 95))
  female   <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.45)
  diabetes <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1.4 + 0.04 * (age - 65)))
  bmi      <- round(rnorm(n, 28, 4.5), 1)
  smoker   <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.25)
  lp_treat <- -0.6 + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 1.0 * diabetes + 0.08 * (bmi - 28) -
    0.3 * female + 0.4 * smoker
  treated <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp_treat))
  lp_death <- log(hr_treat) * treated + 0.06 * (age - 65) + 0.6 * diabetes +
    0.03 * (bmi - 28) - 0.25 * female + 0.55 * smoker
  shape  <- 1.2
  lambda <- 0.05                       # baseline hazard scale (per year)
  t_event <- (-log(runif(n)) / (lambda * exp(lp_death)))^(1 / shape)
  t_admin   <- runif(n, 3, 8)          # study ends 3-8 years after entry
  t_dropout <- rexp(n, rate = 0.04)
  t_cens    <- pmin(t_admin, t_dropout)
  time   <- pmin(t_event, t_cens)
  status <- as.integer(t_event <= t_cens)
  data.frame(
    id       = seq_len(n),
    age, female, diabetes, bmi, smoker,
    treated,
    time     = round(time, 3),
    status
  )
}
cohort <- simulate_cohort(n = 2000, seed = 2026)
set.seed(1)
p_miss <- plogis(-1.5 + 1.5 * cohort$status + 1 * cohort$treated)
cohort_miss <- cohort
cohort_miss$bmi[runif(nrow(cohort)) < p_miss] <- NA
cohort_miss$H <- nelsonaalen(cohort_miss, time, status)
imp_data <- cohort_miss[, c("age", "female", "diabetes", "bmi", "smoker",
                            "treated", "status", "H", "time")]
pred <- make.predictorMatrix(imp_data)
pred[, "time"] <- 0
rm(p_miss)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_mi
#| caption: "Practice: multiple imputation"
imp <- mice(imp_data, m = ______, predictorMatrix = pred,
            seed = 1, printFlag = FALSE)

fit_mi <- with(imp, coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated + age + female +
                            diabetes + bmi + smoker))

summary(______(fit_mi), exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_mi"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1
`m = 5` creates 5 imputed datasets.
:::
:::

::: {.hint exercise="ex_mi"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 2
Rubin's rules are applied by `pool()`.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_mi"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution
```r
imp <- mice(imp_data, m = 5, predictorMatrix = pred,
            seed = 1, printFlag = FALSE)
fit_mi <- with(imp, coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated + age + female +
                            diabetes + bmi + smoker))
summary(pool(fit_mi), exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
```

With 5 imputations, the pooled HR for treatment is about 0.68, much
closer to the full-data value (0.66) than the complete-case estimate (0.50).
With more imputations the result would be a little more stable.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_mi
#| check: true
r <- .result
imp <- .envir_result$imp
if (!inherits(imp, "mids") || imp$m != 5) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Create 5 imputed datasets: <code>m = 5</code>.")
} else if (!inherits(r, "mipo.summary") || !("treated" %in% as.character(r$term)) || r$estimate[as.character(r$term) == "treated"] < 0) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Make the last line <code>summary(pool(fit_mi), exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)</code>.")
} else {
  est <- r$estimate[as.character(r$term) == "treated"]
  list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("Correct! Pooled HR for treatment = %.2f, close to the full-data value of 0.66. The complete-case analysis gave 0.50.", est))
}
```

## Missing data and propensity score matching

Missing confounders cause the same problem for matching: `matchit()`
needs complete data, so the complete cases are matched, with the same
bias:

```{r}
#| label: mt-cc
# matchit() needs complete data, so keep only the complete cases
cc_data <- na.omit(cohort_miss[, c("age", "female", "diabetes", "bmi",
                                   "smoker", "treated", "time", "status")])

m_cc <- matchit(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
                data = cc_data, method = "nearest",
                link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2)
coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated, data = match.data(m_cc),
      robust = TRUE, cluster = subclass) |>
  broom::tidy(exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)
```

The **MatchThem** package matches *within* each imputed dataset, then
pools the results [@pishgar2021]. It works just like `matchit()`, with
`datasets = imp` in place of `data`:

```{r}
#| label: mt-match
mt <- matchthem(treated ~ age + female + diabetes + bmi + smoker,
                datasets = imp, approach = "within",
                method = "nearest", link = "linear.logit", caliper = 0.2)

# Balance, summarised across the 10 imputed datasets
bal.tab(mt, binary = "std", thresholds = c(m = 0.1))
```

```{r}
#| label: mt-pool
fit_mt <- with(mt, coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treated,
                         weights = weights, robust = TRUE,
                         cluster = subclass))
summary(pool(fit_mt), exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)[
  , c("term", "estimate", "2.5 %", "97.5 %")]
```

The complete-case matched HR is 0.56. After multiple imputation and
matching within each dataset, it's **0.75** (95% CI 0.62 to 0.91), close
to the true marginal HR of about 0.73 from Chapter 7.

## Practical advice

- **Look before you analyse.** Count the missing values in each variable,
  and compare patients with and without missing data, as for loss to
  follow-up in @sec-informative.
- **How many imputations?** A common rule of thumb is at least as many as
  the percentage of incomplete cases (here 38%, so about 40). Ten is fine
  for learning. Increase $m$ until the results stop changing.
- **What to include.** Every variable in the analysis model, the outcome
  (`status` and the Nelson–Aalen estimate), and any other variables that
  predict missingness or the missing values.
- **Report it.** Say how much was missing, how you imputed it (method,
  variables, $m$), and compare with the complete-case analysis.
- **MNAR can't be fixed by imputation.** If values are probably missing for
  reasons you didn't record, say so, and consider a sensitivity analysis
  that shifts the imputed values up or down.
- **When is complete-case analysis fine?** When very little is missing
  (a few percent), or when missingness depends only on covariates in the
  model and not on the outcome.

## Summary

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## Key points
- R drops incomplete rows by default (**complete-case analysis**). Always check `n` and `number of events`.
- Missing data are **MCAR**, **MAR** or **MNAR**. If missingness depends on the outcome, complete-case analysis is usually biased.
- **Multiple imputation** fills in the gaps several times, analyses each completed dataset, and **pools** the results with Rubin's rules (`mice()`, `with()`, `pool()`).
- Include the **outcome** in the imputation model: `status` and the **Nelson–Aalen** cumulative hazard (`nelsonaalen()`), not the raw time.
- With propensity score matching, impute first, then match **within** each imputed dataset and pool (**MatchThem**).
- Imputation can't fix MNAR. Report how much was missing and what you did, and compare with the complete-case analysis.
:::

**Answering the question.** By default, R analyses only the complete cases. When missingness depends on the outcome, that can be badly biased: in our example, the treatment HR was 0.50 instead of 0.66. Multiple imputation, including the outcome correctly, gave 0.67, and the same idea combined with matching gave 0.75 against a true marginal value of about 0.73.

## Further reading

All of these are free to read online unless marked otherwise. The whole
book's reading list, grouped by topic, is in @sec-further-reading.

- @sterne2009: **Start here.** A readable guide to multiple imputation, and how it can go wrong.
- @white2009: How to include a survival outcome when imputing covariates for a Cox model (the Nelson–Aalen approach). (May need institutional access.)
- @vanbuuren2018: A free online book by the author of mice, from the basics to advanced topics.
- @pishgar2021: The MatchThem package, for matching and weighting after multiple imputation.
